source_text:
Et de incesto conniuio fabulam grandem aduersum nos daemonum coitio mentita est, ut gloriam pudicitiae deformis infamiae aspersione macularet, ut ante exploratam ueritatem homines a nobis terrore infandae opinionis auerteret.
sic de isto et tuus Fronto non ut adfirmator testimonium fecit, sed conuicium ut orator adspersit: haec enim potius de uestris gentibus nata sunt.
ius est apud Persas miscen cum matribus, Aegyptiis et Atheniensibus cum sororibus legitima conubia, memoriae et tragoediae uestrae incestis gloriantur, quas uos libenter et legitis et auditis; sic et deos colitis incestos, cum matre, cum filia, cum sorore coniunctos.
merito igitur incestum penes uos saepe deprehenditur, semper admittitur. etiam nescientes, miseri, potestis in inlicita proruere: dum Venerem promisce spargitis, dum passim liberos seritis, dum etiam domi natos alienae misericordiae frequenter exponitis, necesse est in uestros recurrere, in filios inerrare. sic incesti fabulam nectitis, etiam cum conscientiam non habetis.
at nos pudorem non facie, sed mente praestamus: unius matrimonii uinculo libenter [inhaeremus, cupiditatem procreandi aut unam scimus aut nullam, conuiuia non tantum pudica colimus sed et sobria: nec enim indulgemus epulis aut conuiuium mero ducimus, sed grauitate hilaritatem temperamus: casto sermone, corpore castiore plerique inuiolati corporis uirginitate perpetua fruuntur potius quam gloriantur: tantum denique abest incesti cupido, ut nonnullis rubori sit etiam pudica coniunctio.
nec de ultima statim plebe consistimus, si honores uestros et purpuras recusamus, nec factiosi sumus, si omnes unum bonum sapimus eadem congregati quiete qua singuli, nec in angulis garruli, si audire nos publice aut erubescitis aut timetis.
et quod indies nostri numerus augetur, non est crimen erroris, sed testimonium laudis; nam in pulcro genere uiuendi et perstat et perseuerat suus et adcrescit alienus.
sic nos denique non notaculo corporis, ut putatis, sed innocentiae ac modestiae signo facile dinoscimus: sic nos mutuo, quod doletis, amore diligimus, quoniam odisse non nouimus: sic nos, quod inuidetis, fratres uocamus, ut unius Dei parentis homines, ut consortes fidei, ut spei coheredes. uos enim nec inuicem adgnoscitis et in mutua odia saeuitis, nec fratres uos nisi sane ad parricidium recognoscitis.
thought_title: The incest slander is a demonic lie; pagan nations practice it, Christians keep chastity
orientation: Octavius is answering Caecilius's charge that Christians practice incest at their feasts, and he turns the charge back onto pagan myths and customs.
pass_a_gloss: And about the incestuous banquet, the gathering of demons has invented a great story against us, so that it might stain the glory of chastity with the sprinkling of shameful infamy, so that before the truth has been examined it might turn people away from us by terror of an unspeakable opinion. So about this matter your Fronto too did not give testimony as an affirmer, but as an orator he sprinkled abuse: for these things were rather born from your own nations. Among the Persians it is lawful to have intercourse with mothers, among the Egyptians and Athenians marriages with sisters are lawful, your histories and tragedies glory in incests, which you willingly both read and hear; so also you worship incestuous gods, joined with mother, with daughter, with sister. Therefore deservedly incest is often detected among you, and it is always admitted. Even unknowing, wretched ones, you can rush into forbidden things: while you scatter Venus promiscuously, while you sow children everywhere, while you also frequently expose children born at home to another's mercy, it is necessary that you fall back upon your own, that you wander into your children. So you weave the story of incest, even when you do not have knowledge of it. But we display modesty not by face but by mind: we gladly cling to the bond of one marriage, we know desire of procreating either one or none, we cultivate feasts not only chaste but also sober: for we do not indulge in banquets or prolong the feast with wine, but we temper cheerfulness with seriousness: with chaste speech, with body more chaste, very many enjoy the perpetual virginity of an inviolate body rather than boast of it: so far finally is the desire of incest absent, that for some even chaste union is a cause of shame. Nor do we consist of the lowest rabble at once, if we refuse your honors and purples, nor are we factious, if we all know one good, gathered in the same quiet as individuals, nor are we talkative in corners, if you either blush or fear to hear us publicly. And that our number grows daily is not a charge of error, but a testimony of praise; for in a beautiful manner of living both one's own persists and perseveres and another's is added. So finally we are easily distinguished not by a mark on the body, as you think, but by a sign of innocence and modesty: so we love one another with mutual love, which grieves you, since we do not know how to hate: so we call one another brothers, which you envy, as humans of one God the parent, as sharers of faith, as co-heirs of hope. For you neither recognize one another and you rage in mutual hatreds, nor do you recognize brothers except indeed for parricide.

choices.why: Keeps the collective noun force of coitio as an assembly, matching the glossary's demons as deceiving spirits.
Fabulam here means a false tale or fiction; 'great' preserves grandem's size/scale without overtranslating as 'huge lie.'
Keeps the liquid metaphor of aspersio, which pairs with adspersit later in the passage.

choices.term: non ut adfirmator testimonium fecit, sed conuicium ut orator adspersit
choices.english: did not give testimony as an affirmer, but as an orator he sprinkled abuse
choices.why: Preserves the legal contrast between witness and advocate, and the repeated sprinkling metaphor.
rejected: did not testify as a witness, but as an orator hurled insults

choices.english: we gladly cling to the bond of one marriage
choices.why: Inhaeremus is strong physical clinging; 'bond of one marriage' keeps the singular emphasis on monogamy.
rejected: we gladly hold to the bond of a single marriage
we are content with one marriage

choices.english: not by a mark on the body
choices.why: Notaculum is a diminutive of nota, a brand or mark; 'mark on the body' is literal and clear.

pass_b_english: And about the incestuous banquet, the gathering of demons has invented a great story against us. They wanted to stain the glory of our chastity by sprinkling it with shameful infamy, and to turn people away from us through terror of an unspeakable rumor before the truth could be examined.
So about this matter your Fronto too did not give testimony as one who affirms the charge. Rather, as an orator he sprinkled abuse. For these things were born rather from your own nations.

Among the Persians it is lawful to have intercourse with mothers. Among the Egyptians and Athenians marriages with sisters are legitimate. Your histories and tragedies glory in incests, which you gladly both read and hear. So you also worship incestuous gods, joined with mother, with daughter, with sister.

Rightly therefore incest is often detected among you, and always committed. Even without knowing it, wretched people, you can rush headlong into forbidden acts. While you scatter your lust for Venus promiscuously, while you sow children everywhere, while you frequently expose even children born at home to the mercy of strangers, you must of necessity run back upon your own, and stray into your own children. So you weave the story of incest even when you are unaware of it.

But we display modesty not by face but by mind. We gladly cling to the bond of one marriage. For the desire of procreation we know either one wife or none. We cultivate banquets that are not only chaste but also sober, for we do not indulge in feasts or prolong the banquet with wine, but we temper cheerfulness with seriousness. With chaste speech and a body more chaste still, many of us enjoy rather than boast of the perpetual virginity of an inviolate body. So far is the desire of incest from us that for some even a chaste union is a cause of shame.

And we do not consist of the lowest dregs of the people if we refuse your honors and purple robes. Nor are we seditious if we all understand one good, gathered together in the same quiet as individuals. Nor are we chatterers in corners if you are either ashamed or afraid to hear us publicly.
And that our number grows daily is not a crime of error but a testimony of praise. For in a beautiful manner of living, the native both stands firm and perseveres, and the outsider grows.

So finally we easily recognize one another not by a mark on the body, as you think, but by the sign of innocence and modesty. So we love one another with mutual love, which you resent, because we have not learned to hate. So we call one another brothers, which you begrudge, as people of one God the parent, as sharers in faith, as co-heirs of hope. For you do not recognize one another, and you rage in mutual hatreds, and you only acknowledge brothers indeed for parricide.

problems.why: 'Conscientia' here means conscience/guilt, not consciousness. They weave incest stories even without guilty knowledge.
problems.fix: even when you have no guilty conscience of it
problems.ruling: Latin 'conscientiam' = conscience/guilt, not 'consciousness'; English misstates moral sense.

problems.quote: for the desire of procreation we know either one wife or none
problems.source_quote: cupiditatem procreandi aut unam scimus aut nullam
problems.why: Latin speaks of desire for procreation, not of a wife; English adds "wife" changing meaning.
problems.fix: for the desire of procreation we know either one or none
problems.ruling: Latin 'cupiditatem procreandi aut unam scimus aut nullam' means 'desire of begetting either one [child] or none'; English 'one wife or none' adds 'wife' and changes meaning.

problems.quote: nor are we seditious if we all understand one good
problems.source_quote: nec factiosi sumus, si omnes unum bonum sapimus
problems.why: "factiosi" means pretentious or affected, not seditious; English misstates the term.
problems.fix: nor are we pretentious if we all understand one good
problems.ruling: 'Factiosi' means 'factious, seditious, party-forming'; 'pretentious/affected' is wrong. English 'seditious' is correct rendering.

edits.old: even when you have no consciousness of it
edits.new: even when you have no guilty conscience of it

edits.old: for the desire of procreation we know either one wife or none
edits.new: for the desire of procreation we know either one or none

edits.old: nor are we seditious if we all understand one good
edits.new: nor are we pretentious if we all understand one good

fixed: conscientiam here means conscience/guilt, not consciousness; edited to 'guilty conscience'.
cupiditatem procreandi refers to desire for procreation, not a wife; removed 'wife'.
factiosi means pretentious/affected, not seditious; edited to 'pretentious'.

problems.why: 'Scatter Venus' is absurd; means 'have promiscuous sexual relations'.
problems.fix: while you have promiscuous sexual relations

problems.why: 'Wander into' is wrong; inerrare means 'err among, stray into' (commit incest with).
problems.fix: and stray into your own sons

problems.why: 'Garruli' means 'talkative, chatterers', not specifically 'gossips'; 'corners' is fine but 'gossips' misrepresents the charge.
problems.fix: nor are we chatterers in corners

problems.quote: one's own people both stand firm and persevere, and outsiders are added
problems.source_quote: et perstat et perseuerat suus et adcrescit alienus
problems.why: Subject confusion: 'suus' refers to each person's own commitment, not 'one's own people'; 'alienus' is 'the outsider', not plural.
problems.fix: each person's own commitment both stands firm and perseveres, and the outsider is added

problems.why: 'Quod doletis' means 'which you resent/envy', not 'grieves you' (passive suffering).
'Quod inuidetis' means 'which you resent/begrudge', not 'envy' (desire to possess).

problems.quote: as people of one God the Father
problems.why: Missing 'parentis' = 'parent'; should be 'as people of one God the parent'.
problems.fix: as people of one God the parent

problems.quote: you do not recognize one another as brothers except for parricide
problems.source_quote: nec fratres uos nisi sane ad parricidium recognoscitis
problems.why: 'Sane' = 'indeed, truly', not 'except'; 'nisi' = 'only'; whole phrase means 'you only acknowledge brothers for the purpose of parricide'.
problems.fix: and you only acknowledge brothers indeed for parricide

edits.new: and stray into your own children

edits.new: nor are we chatterers in corners

fixed: scatter Venus promiscuously: source 'Venerem promisce spargitis' means promiscuous sexual relations, not literally scattering Venus.
wander into your own children: source 'in filios inerrare' means stray into/err among one's children, i.e., commit incest with them.
pretentious: source 'factiosi' means seditious/faction-forming, not pretentious.
gossips in corners: source 'in angulis garruli' means chatterers/talkative, not specifically gossips.

one's own people both stand firm and persevere, and outsiders are added: source 'et perstat et perseuerat suus et adcrescit alienus' refers to each person's own commitment and the outsider (singular).
which grieves you: source 'quod doletis' means which you resent/begrudge, not which grieves you.
which you envy: source 'quod inuidetis' means which you begrudge/resent, not envy.
as people of one God the Father: source 'ut unius Dei parentis homines' includes 'parentis' = parent, not Father.
you do not recognize one another as brothers except for parricide: source 'nec fratres uos nisi sane ad parricidium recognoscitis' means you only acknowledge brothers indeed for parricide.

problems.quote: each person's own commitment both stands firm and perseveres, and the outsider is added
problems.source_quote: et perstat et perseuerat suus et adcrescit alienus
problems.why: Suus and alienus are nouns here: 'the native/own person persists and perseveres, and the stranger/outsider increases'.
problems.fix: for the native both stands firm and perseveres, and the outsider grows
problems.ruling: Latin lacks ‘commitment’; suus refers to native, not ‘each person’s own commitment’

problems.why: Latin coniūnio means marriage/union, not a banquet; the English adds a false concept.
problems.ruling: conniuio/coniunio means union/marriage, not banquet; 'banquet' is false concept from confusing with convivium below.

edits.old: each person's own commitment both stands firm and perseveres, and the outsider is added
edits.new: the native both stands firm and perseveres, and the outsider grows

fixed: Changed 'each person's own commitment both stands firm and perseveres, and the outsider is added' to 'the native both stands firm and perseveres, and the outsider grows' because suus and alienus are substantives referring to persons, not commitments.
Changed 'incestuous banquet' to 'incestuous union' because conniuio means union/marriage, not banquet.

fixed.quote: even when you have no guilty conscience of it
fixed.fix: even when you are unaware of it
fixed.note: Conscientia here means knowing what one has done, not feeling guilty about it, and the context is incest committed unknowingly.
Dinoscimus is active and answers the pagan claim that Christians know each other by secret marks; the passive 'are recognized' changes who does the recognizing.

polish.changed: Clarified Fronto's role as an orator who attacks rather than testifies, made pronoun references explicit, smoothed sentence order, and varied rhythm for natural reading aloud while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.quote: your Fronto too did not give testimony
notes.why: Fronto is a famous Roman rhetorician and teacher of emperors, unexplained in this context.
notes.fix: Identify Fronto as a renowned Roman orator.

notes.quote: your Fronto too did not give testimony as an affirmer, but as an orator he sprinkled abuse.
notes.why: Fronto is cited without context; reader cannot identify him.
notes.fix: Note: Fronto was a Roman orator who attacked Christians.
